### 3 Tips to improve communication for technical audiences


<figcaption>Credit — AI generated by DALL-E mini by craiyon</figcaption>


Most people go straight to building the slides when assigned to do a presentation. People begin by repurposing content from other presentations with the false belief that once the deck is built, the presenter can identify the themes and narrative that motivates the subject. This is like an architect drawing blueprints before she knows the purpose of the building. She may make a beautiful structure, but there is no guarantee the building will be fit for the purpose for which it was intended.

PowerPoints are linear presentation tools. The audience can only see one slide at a time. This makes the medium effective for building an argument logically. Since most audiences request advanced copies of the presentation, using headline page titles can create signposts to help guide viewers through the arguments. Thoughtfully headlined presentations build arguments that progress slowly over time as one point builds on the others. Data points reinforce your key themes and ideas. It also means that you as the presenter have control over what the audience sees and when they see it.

The best graphs, photos, and typography can't make up for lack of thought. New engineers often fall into one of these two traps when creating presentations:

Having only a vague notion of the concept and expecting to figure it out as you go: Conveying an ambiguous message throughout the presentation without considering how the material is meant to contribute to the story they are tasked to tell. It is important to appreciate the difference between having a story and having a collection of data points.

Relying on the audience to decipher the point of a presentation: This puts the burden of discovering the purpose of the presentation on the audience. The role of a presenter is one of a Subject Matter Expert and the audience holds the reasonable expectation to be informed. Leaving the audience to discern the intended message is a dangerous move. Without a clear statement, different audience members can leave the meeting drawing different conclusions.

Fortunately, it doesn't have to be like this. You can craft a story and use powerpoints to present a clear narrative. In fact, you can use any tool you want to communicate a message once you know what it is you're trying to say. So, let's start with how you decide what you want to say.

How to speak strategically: Deciding what you want to say starts from identifying what your audience needs to hear. Where are they? What do they need to know? There is no point in explaining things to people that already understand it or assuming people know things they don't. When you start talking the audience should know where you are coming from and why you are presenting. Every presentation has a purpose that purpose is specific to the audience you're presenting to. If there is not a purpose, then why are you talking?

Analyze your audience prior to the presentation. Think about the priorities and concerns of your audience. Some priorities will be structural (the supervisor showed up because the manager told her to come) and some are emotional (the manager came because she is interested in expanding into a new area) and some are environmental (Your coworker came to support you --- and get free coffee and donuts).

The presentation should begin by acknowledging, and specifically identifying, the audience's priorities and concerns. It is important to build the foundation of the presentation starting with the audience's priorities and concerns.

#### Start analog. For most people, their first step to making a presentation is to open PowerPoint. They may look for other presentation decks that were similar (and the manager may outline the slides she wants when requesting the presentation.) Powerpoint is a useful tool but it focuses the presenter on tactics from the beginning and usually leads to a presentation that lacks a clear central narrative. Instead of diving into the deck, pull out a piece of paper and divide it into four quadrants. In the upper left think about your audience. What are their current feelings about the topic? Why have you been asked to present to them? There must be a reason and you need to clarify what that is. What feelings do they have around the topic (Yes, we said feelings. Those exist in technical organizations too.). The audience could be skeptical of a new program or excited about a recent rumored success. In the upper right, write what you want the audience to know when you are done. How would you like them to feel? What action should they take or not take based on your presentation? In the lower left write the headline for the presentation. What is the real reason for this? It should be a single, powerful sentence. In the bottom right outline the logic flow to move your audience from where they are in the upper left to the goals in the upper right. #### Tell stories, don't just identify topics Most people think in terms of "topics" rather than stories.
